items.title: 4.1.8.4 Types of Graphs; Graph Implementation Using Python

source_refs.note: Topic 4.1.8.4 Types of Graphs with 'Graph Implementation Using Python' (PDF 114-116, printed 111-113). Figures 4.11 and 4.12 are replaced by the original diagram with the same edges and weights. The printed code imports matplotlib as 'pit'; corrected to plt.

items: Directed graph: edges have a direction; you can travel from city A to city B only if an edge points that way (Figure 4.11).
Undirected graph: edges work both ways; if A is friends with B, B is friends with A (Figure 4.12).
Weighted graph: each edge has a weight such as distance, time or cost, which helps find the shortest or quickest route (Figure 4.11).

blocks.alt: Top left: a directed weighted graph on A to E with arrows B to A 10, A to C 12, C to B 20, A to D 60, C to D 32 and E to A 7. Top right: an undirected graph with edges A-B, A-E, B-E, B-D, B-C, C-D and E-D. Bottom left: a tree with root 1, children 2, 3, 4, then 5 and 6 under 2, 7 under 3, 8 and 9 under 4, with DFS and BFS orders. Bottom right: when to use a stack, queue, list, tree or graph.
blocks.caption: Graphs, DFS and BFS, and choosing a structure (original diagram after topics 4.1.8 to 4.3).
blocks.long_description: In the directed weighted graph each edge points one way and carries a cost, for example A to D costs 60 while A to C to D costs 12 + 32 = 44. In the undirected graph every edge works both ways; B touches A, C, D and E, so its degree is 4. On the nine-node tree, DFS with a stack goes deep first: 1, 2, 5, 6, 3, 7, 4, 8, 9, while BFS with a queue goes level by level: 1 to 9 in order. Choose a stack for last-in-first-out work, a queue for first-in-first-out, a list for ordered collections, a tree for hierarchies and a graph for networks.

blocks.title: Python code (each .... is one 4-space indent)
blocks.text:
import networkx as nx
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
G = nx.Graph()          # create a graph
G.add_node("A")
G.add_node("B")
G.add_node("C")
G.add_edge("A", "B")     # add edges
G.add_edge("B", "C")
nx.draw(G, with_labels=True)
plt.show()
The code creates a graph with three nodes and two edges using the NetworkX library and draws it with Matplotlib (both must be installed).

blocks.prompt: In the directed weighted graph (B to A 10, A to C 12, C to B 20, A to D 60, C to D 32, E to A 7), what is the cheapest way from E to D?
blocks.explanation: E to A to C to D costs 7 + 12 + 32 = 51, cheaper than E to A to D, 7 + 60 = 67.

items: Graph types: directed (one-way), undirected (two-way), weighted (costs); NetworkX builds and draws graphs.
